The 'sovereignty' Bitcoin enables is real but does require some user education and discipline — there is no customer service to call if you lose your keys.

questions.question: Strike (founded by Jack Mallers, 2017) and Cash App's Bitcoin features have driven significant retail Bitcoin adoption in the US. Strike's approach to international remittances uses Bitcoin's Lightning Network as a settlement layer. What's distinctive about Strike's design?
questions.answer: Senders pay in their local currency, recipients receive in theirs — Bitcoin moves between them invisibly as the settlement rail, far cheaper than Western Union or SWIFT alternatives
choices: Senders pay in their local currency, recipients receive in theirs — Bitcoin moves between them invisibly as the settlement rail, far cheaper than Western Union or SWIFT alternatives
All transactions are denominated only in Bitcoin — Strike does not support any fiat currency interaction and requires users to hold BTC for any service
Strike requires Federal Reserve approval — every Strike transaction is reviewed by the Fed's payments division before execution and clearance
Strike runs on Ethereum — not Bitcoin — and uses smart contracts to settle remittances through the Solana high-speed parallel blockchain
questions.context: Lightning Network-based remittance services like Strike have demonstrated practical Bitcoin utility beyond store-of-value use cases. Mallers became a public advocate for Bitcoin Lightning integration in El Salvador. The Lightning-as-rail model lets users interact with familiar local currencies while Bitcoin handles the cross-border value transfer in seconds at minimal cost.

questions.question: Casey Rodarmor launched the Ordinals protocol on Bitcoin in January 2023, exploiting the Taproot upgrade to inscribe arbitrary data (text, images) onto individual satoshis. By summer 2023 millions of inscriptions had been created. What's the debate?
questions.answer: Inscriptions raised transaction fees and block-space usage — improving miner revenue, but critics argue they distract from Bitcoin's monetary purpose and clog blocks with arbitrary data
choices: Inscriptions raised transaction fees and block-space usage — improving miner revenue, but critics argue they distract from Bitcoin's monetary purpose and clog blocks with arbitrary data
Inscriptions are illegal under SEC regulation — Rodarmor was charged in 2023 and the entire Ordinals protocol was shut down by federal court order
Inscriptions are mandatory for all Bitcoin transactions — every block since 2023 must contain at least one inscription under updated protocol requirements
Inscriptions replaced Bitcoin's monetary purpose — the protocol no longer functions as money since the Ordinals launch took over all block capacity
questions.context: Ordinals brought NFT-style functionality to Bitcoin — without altering the protocol, simply by encoding data into Taproot witness data. Bitcoin's community has not reached consensus on whether Ordinals are beneficial (raising fees, demonstrating use cases) or distracting (taking up block space, raising fees for monetary use). The debate continues; the protocol works either way.

questions.question: Bitcoin's price has moved through remarkable milestones since 2009. First market exchange (May 2010, Pizza Day): 10,000 BTC for ~$25 (less than a penny per BTC). $1 (February 2011). $1,000 (November 2013). $10,000 (November 2017). $69,000 (November 2021 peak). $73,000 (March 2024). What's the broader pattern?
questions.answer: Long-term appreciation punctuated by 70-90% drawdowns — Bitcoin's volatility is high but the upward trend across cycles reflects growing recognition of fixed-supply digital scarcity
choices: Long-term appreciation punctuated by 70-90% drawdowns — Bitcoin's volatility is high but the upward trend across cycles reflects growing recognition of fixed-supply digital scarcity
Steady linear growth without volatility — Bitcoin has appreciated about 10% per year consistently with no significant drawdowns since 2009
A single bubble in 2017 — Bitcoin has had no meaningful price movement before or after that single event in November 2017 alone
Government-controlled pricing — the US Federal Reserve sets Bitcoin's price quarterly via FOMC meetings, with no market involvement at all
questions.context: Bitcoin's volatility is genuinely high — annual drawdowns of 30-50% are normal, and 70-90% drawdowns have occurred multiple times. Long-term holders ('HODLers') have generally benefited from holding through volatility. The asset's market cap (sometimes over $1 trillion) reflects substantial institutional and retail adoption since 2017. Whether the volatility decreases over time as adoption matures remains an open question.

questions.question: 'Bitcoin maximalism' is the view that Bitcoin is uniquely sound money among cryptocurrencies and that other cryptos are scams, speculation, or experiments with worse trade-offs. What's the maximalist argument distinguishing Bitcoin from 'crypto' generally?
questions.answer: Bitcoin had a credibly-neutral, anonymous launch with no pre-mine, no founder allocation, no central control — features that no major altcoin can claim, and that are essential to sound money
choices: Bitcoin had a credibly-neutral, anonymous launch with no pre-mine, no founder allocation, no central control — features that no major altcoin can claim, and that are essential to sound money
Bitcoin is technically identical to all altcoins — the maximalist position is purely tribal loyalty and has no economic or technical foundation whatsoever
Bitcoin uses the same proof-of-stake consensus as altcoins — there is no meaningful difference in design philosophy between Bitcoin and Ethereum or others
Bitcoin is centralized at the Bitcoin Foundation — making it identical to centralized cryptocurrencies, with no special claim to decentralization or fairness
questions.context: The 'immaculate conception' framing — Satoshi's anonymous launch, no pre-mine, the Genesis block's provably-unspendable coins — is unique to Bitcoin among major cryptocurrencies. Maximalists argue this matters because money requires credibility that founders, marketing teams, and venture capitalists undermine. Critics argue maximalism is too strict — useful innovation can come from other projects. The debate is ongoing.

questions.question: Liquid is a sidechain launched by Blockstream in 2018 — a Bitcoin Layer 2 designed for exchanges and institutional users. Liquid uses a federated trust model (15 functionaries) rather than Bitcoin's open mining model. What's the trade-off?
questions.answer: Faster settlement, confidential transactions, asset issuance — but at the cost of trusting the federation, a weaker security model than the main Bitcoin chain offers
choices: Faster settlement, confidential transactions, asset issuance — but at the cost of trusting the federation, a weaker security model than the main Bitcoin chain offers
Liquid has stronger security than Bitcoin — the federated model is more decentralized than Bitcoin's open mining model in every measurable respect
Liquid is identical to Bitcoin in every way — there is no meaningful design distinction between the two networks despite different consensus mechanisms
Liquid replaces Bitcoin entirely — institutional users adopted Liquid as their primary network in 2018 and abandoned the original Bitcoin chain at that point
questions.context: Liquid serves exchanges that need faster, more private settlement than Bitcoin's base chain offers. It's a specialized tool with a specific use case, not a general replacement for Bitcoin. The federated security model is honestly disclosed — users opt into the trust assumption. Other Layer 2 approaches (Lightning, statechains, drivechains) offer different trade-offs.

questions.question: Satoshi Nakamoto's last known public communication was an email to Bitcoin developer Mike Hearn in April 2011, saying 'I've moved on to other things' and noting Bitcoin was 'in good hands' with Gavin Andresen. Months earlier, in December 2010, Satoshi had stepped back from the Bitcoin forum. Why was this exit timing notable?
questions.answer: WikiLeaks had begun accepting Bitcoin donations in late 2010 after PayPal cut them off — drawing US government attention that may have prompted Satoshi's withdrawal
choices: WikiLeaks had begun accepting Bitcoin donations in late 2010 after PayPal cut them off — drawing US government attention that may have prompted Satoshi's withdrawal
Bitcoin had reached the $1,000 price level — Satoshi withdrew after a lucrative public sale of his coins in December 2010 at the early peak
Mt. Gox had collapsed in late 2010 — Satoshi blamed himself for the exchange's failure and withdrew from public participation entirely
Satoshi died in late 2010 — his identity is now believed to be Hal Finney, who passed away from ALS at that time according to most analysts
questions.context: Hal Finney died in August 2014, not 2010. Mt. Gox collapsed in 2014, not 2010. The WikiLeaks connection is documented — Satoshi explicitly warned against the project accepting Bitcoin donations because of the attention it would draw. His withdrawal correlates with the increased visibility. Satoshi mined large amounts of Bitcoin in 2009-2010 that have never moved — likely held by him or unrecoverable.

questions.question: Brazil's securities regulator (CVM) approved the world's first equity-fund Bitcoin ETF in March 2021 — the QR Asset Management QBTC11, traded on B3 (Brazil's stock exchange). Canada had approved a similar product (Purpose Bitcoin ETF) in February 2021. The US lagged until January 2024. Why did multiple jurisdictions approve before the US?
questions.answer: Their regulatory frameworks were more flexible — the US SEC required extensive evidence of market-manipulation safeguards before approving spot Bitcoin products domestically
choices: Their regulatory frameworks were more flexible — the US SEC required extensive evidence of market-manipulation safeguards before approving spot Bitcoin products domestically
Brazil and Canada had banned Bitcoin entirely — the ETF approvals were administrative errors that were later reversed within months of issuance
The US had approved Bitcoin ETFs earliest — in 2017, several years before Canada and Brazil entered the regulated cryptocurrency-fund market
All three countries approved on the same day — there was no meaningful difference in regulatory timing between the US, Brazil, and Canada
questions.context: Earlier US Bitcoin futures-based ETFs (like ProShares BITO, October 2021) traded futures contracts rather than direct Bitcoin holdings. The spot Bitcoin ETF approvals in the US (January 2024) followed years of regulatory resistance and a federal court ruling that the SEC's earlier denials were 'arbitrary and capricious.' Brazil's QBTC11 was a small product but a significant precedent.

questions.question: Bitcoin's governance is distinctive: there is no single decision-making body. Changes require coordination among many stakeholder groups — developers, miners, node operators, exchanges, users. Even consensus rules can only be changed if enough nodes adopt the new code. What's the practical effect?
questions.answer: Major changes happen slowly and conservatively — Bitcoin's protocol has remained remarkably stable for fifteen years, with no central party able to push through unwanted changes
choices: Major changes happen slowly and conservatively — Bitcoin's protocol has remained remarkably stable for fifteen years, with no central party able to push through unwanted changes
The Bitcoin Foundation makes all decisions — every protocol change requires Foundation approval and members vote on each Bitcoin Improvement Proposal
The largest mining pool sets policy — whichever pool has the most hashrate makes all Bitcoin decisions through a monthly chairman-of-the-board process
The Federal Reserve regulates Bitcoin — every protocol change must be approved by the Federal Reserve's payments division before implementation
questions.context: Bitcoin's stability is a feature, not a bug — money requires predictable rules people can trust over decades. Each major upgrade (P2SH, SegWit, Taproot) has been deliberated for years and required broad coordination. The protocol's resistance to change is intentional. Critics call it sluggish; defenders call it disciplined.

questions.question: Andreas Antonopoulos — born in London, raised in Greece, settled in California — became a leading popular Bitcoin educator from around 2013. Mastering Bitcoin (2014) is his technical reference; The Internet of Money series (2016-2019) collects his more philosophical talks. What's his recurring theme?
questions.answer: Bitcoin is not just digital cash but a new kind of money — separating money from the state for the first time since governments monopolized currency, with enormous implications
choices: Bitcoin is not just digital cash but a new kind of money — separating money from the state for the first time since governments monopolized currency, with enormous implications
Bitcoin is a short-term speculation only — Antonopoulos argues Bitcoin has no long-term significance and will be replaced by altcoins within a decade
Bitcoin is a Federal Reserve project — Antonopoulos argues the protocol was developed by US central bankers as a tool for monetary surveillance
Bitcoin is identical to gold — Antonopoulos argues the two assets are interchangeable and there is no meaningful distinction between physical and digital money
questions.context: Antonopoulos refused to monetize his role in obvious ways — he didn't pre-mine altcoins or push ICOs. After receiving large Bitcoin donations from his community in 2017, his integrity was reinforced rather than corrupted. His public-speaking work has helped explain Bitcoin to general audiences. Mastering Bitcoin remains a standard technical introduction.

questions.question: Bitcoin is often called 'digital gold' — Saifedean Ammous popularized this in The Bitcoin Standard (2018). The metaphor draws on gold's monetary properties: scarcity, durability, divisibility, fungibility, portability, verifiability. What's Bitcoin's advantage over gold?
questions.answer: Bitcoin is more portable — sendable anywhere in minutes, divisible to 1/100,000,000 of a coin, and each transaction is cryptographically provable, all beyond physical gold's reach
choices: Bitcoin is more portable — sendable anywhere in minutes, divisible to 1/100,000,000 of a coin, and each transaction is cryptographically provable, all beyond physical gold's reach
Bitcoin has no advantage over gold — physical gold remains superior on every monetary dimension regardless of technological advances in the digital era
Bitcoin has the same weight as gold — both metals are equally portable and require the same cost to transport across international borders
Bitcoin's only advantage is government endorsement — central banks prefer Bitcoin over gold and have switched their reserves to BTC since 2020
questions.context: The 'digital gold' framing captures Bitcoin's monetary properties — but it's also a simplification. Bitcoin's history is shorter than gold's, its volatility is higher, and its 21M cap is a different kind of scarcity than gold's geological scarcity. The Bitcoin Standard makes the case that Bitcoin will eventually monetize as global sound money. Whether that happens — and on what time horizon — remains an open question.

questions.question: Bitcoin's adoption arc has run from cypherpunk obscurity in 2009 to Wall Street institutionalization by 2024. BlackRock's IBIT, Fidelity's FBTC, and other spot ETFs hold over a million BTC combined. MicroStrategy under Michael Saylor holds over 200,000 BTC. What does institutional adoption represent?
questions.answer: Recognition that Bitcoin is here to stay — and that traditional financial institutions need exposure to programmable digital scarcity, even at the cost of changing their long-standing positions
choices: Recognition that Bitcoin is here to stay — and that traditional financial institutions need exposure to programmable digital scarcity, even at the cost of changing their long-standing positions
A government takeover of Bitcoin — the SEC nationalized Bitcoin in 2023 and major Wall Street firms hold it on behalf of the US Treasury Department
The end of Bitcoin's monetary mission — institutional adoption proved Bitcoin had failed at its cypherpunk goals and become just another Wall Street product
Coincidence — there is no causal connection between Wall Street ETF approvals in 2024 and any prior Bitcoin development since 2009 forward
questions.context: The cypherpunk-to-Wall-Street arc is one of the more remarkable trajectories in modern finance. The protocol Satoshi launched anonymously in 2008-2009 with no foundation, no central party, and no marketing budget is now held in corporate treasuries and offered through major investment firms. The transition raises interesting questions about whether institutional adoption complements or undermines Bitcoin's original purpose.
